prize_parts.citation: for showing how firm heterogeneity and selection into exporting shape trade patterns, reallocation across firms and the gains from trade

statement.case_for: Melitz (2003) moved trade theory from the industry to the firm. It explains why only some firms export, why exporters differ systematically from non-exporters, and how liberalisation raises aggregate productivity through reallocation. This is a new channel for gains from trade, distinct from comparative advantage and from scale and variety. Helpman supplied much of the surrounding architecture, including Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple on exporting versus FDI, so a two-name credit follows the intellectual structure of the contribution. More than two decades of firm-level evidence across many countries have tested the mechanism and refined its parametric details without displacing the core insight. The paradigm now disciplines empirical work and policy evaluation in trade. After listening to colleagues I move B010 ahead of B037, my opening first choice. The scientific case for B037 is strong, but the attribution problem that nearly every opening statement flagged, mine included, is a real obstacle under a three-name cap. B010 has no comparable problem.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is credit. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, and Hopenhayn in firm dynamics, are real precursors or parallel contributors who are not credited on this ballot, and the Eaton-Kortum strand sits outside this entry. A Helpman-Melitz award leaves them out, and Redding as well. A second reservation is that the quantitative size of the selection gains depends on parametric assumptions such as Pareto productivity draws. A third is that trade was recognised in 2008 for new trade theory, so the Committee should confirm that this is a distinct advance rather than an extension.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B010 first. He sees Melitz as the central model and Helpman as a major parallel and extending contributor. He also asks whether Eaton-Kortum or the Bernard-Jensen exporter-premium pioneers would have to be credited alongside, which would fragment the credit.
responses.response: I agree on the core. I would qualify the worry about fragmentation. Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum documented exporter facts and built quantitative frameworks that are important, but the selection-and-reallocation mechanism and its welfare implications are what make this a discovery, and those are carried by Melitz (2003) and Helpman's firm-level work. The omission is a real cost that the citation wording should not hide. I do not think it makes the two-name credit unsafe. I note that Hassler and I are co-authors on a recent unrelated paper, so my agreement should not be read as deference.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B010 sixth. He asks whether it is a distinct advance beyond the new trade theory recognised in 2008, and whether Redding or the Bernard-Jensen exporter facts should be included.
responses.response: The 2008 prize recognised monopolistic competition, scale and trade patterns with representative firms. Melitz changed the unit of analysis, so the gains come from selection and reallocation across heterogeneous firms. The empirical agenda that followed is different in kind. I accept that the two are related. I do not think the 2008 prize covers this contribution. On Redding, I think his work is better described as a successor in quantitative and spatial trade than a co-origin, and I would keep him out of the core pair.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B037 first with Calvo, Taylor and Woodford, as the foundational pricing mechanism, the policy rule and the integrated normative framework. He accepts that a three-person cut omits Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets.
responses.response: I ranked B037 first as well, so I take the case seriously. My own triad was Woodford, Taylor and Gali, while his is Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. Each of us drew a defensible boundary, and the two boundaries differ by one name. That shows the credit is unstable, and a prize citation would have to defend the choice against Calvo, Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and Gertler. The post-2021 inflation also leaves open how well the baseline model performed. I therefore keep B037 as my first alternative and not as my preferred part. If the Committee finds a principled triad, I would reopen this.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B019 first. He sees a clean two-person credit for Kiyotaki and Moore and a foundational mechanism in macro-finance that does not depend on one field's taste.
responses.response: I agree that the Kiyotaki-Moore attribution is clean and that the mechanism is foundational. I ranked it fifth for two reasons. The 2022 prize on banks and financial crises is adjacent, and the empirical identification of the collateral amplification channel is more indirect than the theory's influence suggests. Teorell himself lists the overlap with the 2022 prize as an uncertainty, so we may differ more in weighting than in substance. I would not oppose B019 if the Committee judges it distinct from the 2022 work, but I do not rank it above B010.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee wants to credit Bernard, Eaton, Jensen or Kortum alongside Helpman and Melitz, and whether the three-name cap or the ballot's credited list prevents it.
How sensitive the measured gains from selection are to parametric assumptions, such as the Pareto productivity distribution.
Whether B037 can be given a principled three-person boundary. If it can, my ranking of it relative to B010 could change.
Whether the 2008 trade prize and the 2022 and 2024 prizes affect how the Committee weighs field balance.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to any credited candidate is apparent from my profile. I disclose field proximity: my research is in international trade and industrial organisation, including price-setting and exchange-rate pass-through, which is close to B010, B003 and the pricing side of B037. I co-authored a 2026 IJIO paper with Hassler (chair) and Ellingsen, neither of whom is a candidate. My spouse's public political role is noted as a public fact and has no apparent bearing on this ballot.
